title: Room 402
text:
It was the second Saturday in August and the hotel was fully booked. At 9 pm a couple arrived with a valid reservation and a booking reference. The system showed no room.

The hotel was overbooked by one. It happens, usually because of a no-show that never happens.

The receptionist, Petya, had two options. Explain the policy, or solve the problem. She did the second thing first and the explaining afterwards.

She called a partner hotel four minutes away, booked their last available room, and paid for the taxi. Then she came back to the desk and told the couple exactly what had happened, without hiding behind the word "system".

She also promised them room 402 for the following night, a sea view, at the rate they had originally booked.

They were not happy. They were, however, treated like adults.

The next morning they moved in, stayed four more nights, and left a review that mentioned Petya by name. The line the manager remembered was this one: they told us the truth before we had to ask twice.

Overbooking costs a hotel money. Pretending it didn't happen costs more.

questions.q: Why was there no room for the couple?
options: They arrived on the wrong date
Found and paid for another hotel and taxi

questions.q: What did she promise for the following night?
options: Room 402 with a sea view at the original rate
A room at the partner hotel
Being told the truth without having to ask

title: 140 covers and one allergy
text:
Saturday night, 140 covers booked, and the restaurant was two waiters short because of illness.

At 7:40 a table of six was seated. One guest mentioned a nut allergy while ordering drinks. The waiter wrote it on the ticket in red, as the rule requires, and repeated it to the kitchen out loud.

At 8:20 the pastry chef, who had come in on his day off to help, plated a dessert with a hazelnut crumb. It was the standard plating. He had not seen the ticket, because desserts were being fired from a printer at the other end of the pass.

The head chef caught it as the plate left the pass. Nobody was harmed.

The restaurant changed one thing the following week. Allergy tickets are now printed on both stations and a second person reads them back before service. It adds about eight seconds per table.

The owner explained it simply at the staff meeting. On the busiest night of the year, with the best people in the building, the system nearly failed. That is exactly when a system has to work, and eight seconds is a cheap price.

options: Written in red on the ticket and said aloud to the kitchen
Entered into the booking system only

questions.q: Why did the pastry chef miss the allergy?
options: Dessert tickets printed at a different station
He was not told about the table
He could not read the handwriting

questions.q: What was the outcome that night?
options: The head chef stopped the plate; nobody was harmed

questions.q: What is the owner's main argument?
options: Systems must work on the hardest nights, so a small cost is worth it
